name: IRONLIMB VertebraCore T7 Spinal Column
product_name: IRONLIMB VertebraCore T7 Spinal Column Reinforcement
description:
The VertebraCore T7 replaces damaged or at-risk vertebrae with precision-machined titanium-alloy segments bonded to remaining organic tissue via osseointegration pins. A continuous load-distribution rail runs the length of the implant, redirecting compressive and shear forces away from the spinal cord. Integrated pressure sensors feed real-time data to a subcutaneous microprocessor that detects dangerous loading conditions and triggers muscular bracing signals. Anti-paralysis protocols actively monitor cord impingement and can decompress via micro-actuated spacer expansion.

The T7 is the standard-issue spinal implant for heavy laborers, freight handlers, and warehouse workers throughout the Shelf and Slab tiers who can't afford downtime from injury. Ironlimb markets it aggressively to industrial employers as a liability reduction tool, and many Fenris Industrial and Port Authority workers receive it as a workplace stipend. It carries zero social cachet — nobody brags about an Ironlimb spine — but it has kept thousands of workers upright who would otherwise be paralyzed.
installation_requirements: Spinal surgery under general anesthesia, 6-8 hour procedure, certified neurosurgical team, 4-week recovery minimum
rejection_risk: Moderate — titanium osseointegration can fail in patients with poor bone density or chronic inflammation; immunosuppressants recommended for 90 days post-op
maintenance: Annual imaging scan, quarterly sensor calibration, microprocessor firmware update every 18 months

cultural_context: Among Shelf-tier workers, an Ironlimb spine is a quiet badge of survival — the physical record of an injury survived or a life of brutal labor. It is neither glamorous nor stigmatized; it is simply the thing that keeps you working.

story_hooks: A worker's VertebraCore anti-paralysis alert keeps firing without cause — either the sensor is malfunctioning or someone is deliberately inducing spinal stress via a hidden signal
An employer is quietly mandating the T7 for all new hires as a 'safety benefit,' but the microprocessor firmware contains undisclosed productivity monitoring and compliance override features
